headings.text: The core rmapi — hub and integration point

blocks.html:
A shallow conceptual map of how Deploy App fits together: it names the moving parts and how they relate, but does not go deep into any one component. For shared vocabulary see the Glossary; to pick a stack see Choose your platform; for component-level Kubernetes detail see the Develop Deploy App book.

The shape of the system

Deploy App is one identity provider, one hub API, a web UI, several products, and a certificate/trust layer that lets them talk securely. A user enrolls once, authenticates with an mTLS client certificate, and reaches every product they are entitled to. The hub fans user-lifecycle events out to each product over mTLS, so revoking a user in one place revokes them everywhere.

The same shape runs on both stacks; only the ingress and the CA / trust layer differ — so here is one diagram per stack.

Legacy (Docker Compose) — nginx ingress (certs via miniwerk) in front of the hub, with CFSSL as the internal CA:

blocks.html:
Where a component lives differs by stack. On legacy (Docker Compose) the parts are git submodules of docker-rasenmaeher-integration; on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform, alpha) they are Kustomize bases/overlays and operators. See Choose your platform for the full comparison — this page does not repeat it.

Identity (Keycloak)

Keycloak is the identity provider and the source of truth for users, groups, and roles. It backs the single login flow that all products share, with OpenLDAP bridging to products that speak LDAP rather than OIDC (notably TAK). On legacy it is reachable on the kc. subdomain; on Kubernetes it runs via the keycloak-operator. Group/role management is increasingly surfaced inside Deploy App itself rather than the Keycloak admin UI.

The core rmapi — hub and integration point

The core rmapi (rasenmaeher_api, from pvarki/python-rasenmaeher-api) is the hub and the most security-critical component. It owns user CRUD and the Deploy App operations, and it is the single point every integration connects to. When a user is created, approved, promoted, demoted, or revoked, the core rmapi fans those events out to each registered product integration API over mTLS, and reflects certificate operations into the CA.

On legacy it runs as the rmapi compose service; on Kubernetes as deployment/opendefense-rmapi in the opendefense-system namespace. For its endpoints, see the API reference.

Product integration APIs

Each product is fronted by a small product integration API that the core rmapi drives. It exposes user-lifecycle endpoints which the core rmapi calls over mTLS, and reflects each event into the underlying product — acting as a translation layer between the hub and the product. Shipped examples are Matrix (pvarki/python-matrix-rmapi), TAK (pvarki/python-tak-rmapi), and MediaMTX (pvarki/python-mediamtx-rmmtxauthz); new ones start from pvarki/python-integration-template. See the Build an Integration book for the full workflow.

The service an integrator builds is a product integration API, never "rmapi" — that name belongs only to the core RASENMAEHER API.

On legacy, product integration APIs are reached on the product integration APIs port **4626** behind a mtls.<product>.<domain> subdomain, and the product is registered with miniwerk via MW_PRODUCTS so it gets a subdomain and certificate.

Certificate authority and trust

Everything internal is secured with mTLS, so a CA and a trust-distribution mechanism are central — and this is where the two stacks differ most.

  • Legacy: CFSSL (pvarki/docker-rasenmaeher-cfssl) is the internal CA, reached only over the restricted canet network; miniwerk handles the public-facing Let's Encrypt certificates and subdomain wiring.
  • Kubernetes: cert-manager issues certificates, trust-manager distributes the trust bundle, and opendefense-pki holds the CA. There is no CFSSL and no miniwerk here.

The CA private key is the system's top "crown jewel": compromising it means total identity compromise for an instance. Network isolation and (planned) CA-call authentication keep it off the open path. See the Deploy App runbook's Threat Model for the trust boundaries and attack trees.

Ingress

Ingress is how external traffic reaches the UI, the core rmapi, and each product. It terminates TLS, enforces mTLS on protected paths, and is the first line of defense.

  • Legacy: nginx, configured by miniwerk (which also owns the subdomain scheme and MW_PRODUCTS).
  • Kubernetes: Traefik.

Supporting pieces (Kubernetes)

On the Kubernetes stack, supporting infrastructure runs as operators rather than plain containers: cloudnative-pg (Postgres), keycloak-operator, external-secrets-operator, Traefik, and storage/monitoring operators. They are deployed in ordered phases before the application services. The legacy stack runs the equivalents (PostgreSQL, OpenLDAP, OCSP responder) as plain compose services.

Going deeper

This page is intentionally shallow. For the detailed Kubernetes component breakdown — manifest layout, phasing, operators, and per-service folders — see the Develop Deploy App book. For operating concerns (the deployment diagram, threat model, and audit logging), see the Operate book and the Deploy App runbook.
